posts.title: Connecting Early Action protocols to Early Warning Systems
posts.excerpt: If the objective of an early warning system is to save lives and protect assets, then no degree of perfection in hazard observation or message dissemination will matter if people don't know what to do.
content:
There are some really obvious problems with how early warning sytems work. One of them relates to the fact that people do not necessarily know what to do when an alert is issued.

Let's say you're responsible for operations at courier service or logistics operator. The warning says

Incidentally, that would already be a better warning than you'd get in most contexts.

There's a peculiar paradox at the heart of contemporary digital design: we have never had more tools, more frameworks, more possibilities at our fingertips—and yet the most compelling work often emerges from radical constraint.

I've been thinking about this while working on a recent project. The client wanted 'everything'—animations, gradients, custom cursors, parallax scrolling. The usual wishlist. But somewhere in the conversation, I asked a different question: What if we did less?

Every new CSS property, every JavaScript library, every design trend whispers the same seductive promise: you could use this. You should use this. Everyone else is using this. The fear of being left behind is real.

content.alt: A minimal designer workspace with a single plant

content: But mastery isn't about using every tool in the box. It's about knowing which three tools will do the job with grace and precision. It's about the confidence to let the page breathe, to trust whitespace, to resist the urge to fill every pixel with meaning.

content.text: Perfection is achieved not when there is nothing more to add, but when there is nothing left to take away. — Antoine de Saint-Exupéry

content: This applies to more than just aesthetics. Restraint in our technical choices—fewer dependencies, simpler architectures, semantic HTML—creates resilient systems that age gracefully rather than crumbling under the weight of their own complexity.
What would happen if we approached each project by asking not 'What can we add?' but 'What can we remove?' What if our default position was simplicity, and every addition required justification?

I'm not advocating for minimalism as an aesthetic—though I confess a personal weakness for it. I'm suggesting restraint as a practice. As a discipline. As a way of making work that respects the people who encounter it.

Because at the end of the day, restraint is generosity. It's saying: I won't waste your time, your attention, your bandwidth. I've thought carefully about what matters here, and I've removed everything that doesn't.
That, I think, is the real craft.

posts.title: Building Systems That Last
posts.excerpt: Software has a lifespan problem. We build for today and hope for tomorrow. What if we designed for decades instead?
content: Most software is built like a sandcastle. Beautiful, intricate, doomed. We know it won't last, but we build it anyway, promising ourselves we'll refactor later, that we'll pay down the technical debt, that this time will be different.
It never is.

I recently inherited a codebase from 2018. Six years old. Ancient by web standards. The framework was deprecated, the dependencies had security warnings, the build process required a specific version of Node that no one remembered why.
Six years. That's how long it took for something that probably took months to build to become essentially archaeological.
Meanwhile, there's a Roman aqueduct in Segovia that's been carrying water for 2,000 years. What does it know that we don't?
The aqueduct doesn't rely on any particular framework. It understands gravity, materials, and load distribution. It's built on principles that don't change.
Our industry has gotten very good at patterns—design patterns, architectural patterns, framework-specific patterns. But patterns are fashion. They come and go. Principles endure.

Here's what I'm trying now: Before reaching for a framework, library, or abstraction, I ask whether I understand the underlying principle well enough to build it from scratch if I had to. If not, I learn the principle first.
It's slower. It feels inefficient. But the code that emerges is comprehensible, maintainable, and less likely to become legacy the moment the framework community moves on to the next big thing.
We won't build software that lasts 2,000 years. But maybe we can do better than six.

posts.title: Notes on Typography and Rhythm
posts.excerpt: Why some pages feel like they breathe while others suffocate. A brief exploration of vertical rhythm and typographic hierarchy.
content: You can feel it even if you can't name it. Some pages invite you in. Others push you away. The difference often comes down to rhythm.

Not the kind of rhythm you hear. The kind you see. Or rather, the kind you feel as your eye moves down the page, finding a predictable cadence in the spacing, the weight changes, the subtle variations in scale.

Vertical rhythm is the practice of aligning all elements to a consistent baseline grid. It's the typographic equivalent of a drummer keeping time—mostly invisible, but its absence is immediately felt.

content.alt: Comparison of text with and without baseline grid

content: When your line height, margins, and padding all respect the same underlying rhythm, the page develops a visual breathing pattern. White space becomes intentional rather than accidental. The eye knows where to rest.

content.text: Good typography is invisible. Great typography is felt.

content: But rhythm alone isn't enough. You need contrast. Variation. A way to signal importance without shouting.

This is where modular scales come in—mathematical relationships between font sizes that feel harmonious rather than arbitrary. The golden ratio. Perfect fourths. Major thirds. Each creates a different personality, a different emotional register.

I've been using a 1.25 scale lately (major third). It's assertive without being aggressive. Confident without being loud. It matches the tone I'm trying to set in my work: serious but not somber, clear but not clinical.
These aren't rules. They're instruments. Learn to play them, and you can make almost anything sing.
